questions.q: What is the most important thing that defines a deployment environment, beyond its name?
options: The programming language used to write its deployment script
The color used to label it in the pipeline dashboard
How many servers it physically contains
The rules attached to it — which secrets are available, who must approve, and which branches can target it
questions.explain: Two environments can run identical infrastructure but behave completely differently in a pipeline because of the rules — secrets, approvals, branch restrictions — attached to their names.

questions.q: In the dev → staging → production sequence, what is staging's main purpose?
options: To permanently store old versions of the application
To be the first place every merge lands, with no expectations of stability
To replace the need for a production environment entirely
To closely mirror production's configuration and exercise a release against realistic data before real customer traffic touches it
questions.explain: Staging is a production-like rehearsal environment — close enough in configuration to catch problems before a release reaches real users.

questions.q: In the workflow `deploy-production: needs: deploy-staging`, what does `needs:` enforce?
options: Nothing — needs: is purely cosmetic in the Actions UI
That deploy-production deletes the staging environment once it starts
That deploy-production and deploy-staging run at the same time
That deploy-production only starts after deploy-staging has succeeded, preventing any path that skips staging
questions.explain: needs: creates a dependency chain, so production can only be reached by first passing through staging successfully.

questions.q: In Azure DevOps, where do environments appear as a feature?
options: As a first-class object under Pipelines → Environments, tracking every run that has targeted them regardless of which pipeline triggered the run
They don't exist in Azure DevOps, only in GitHub Actions
Only inside a Dockerfile
As a column in the work item backlog
questions.explain: Azure DevOps exposes environments as their own object in the pipelines UI, independent of any single pipeline definition.

questions.q: Why do production environments typically have stricter rules than dev or staging, even when the deployment command is identical?
options: Stricter rules are a historical convention with no practical reasoning behind them
Production holds real customer data and has real consequences for downtime, unlike dev's disposable nature or staging's realistic-but-not-real data
Production servers run a different operating system
Production environments cannot use kubectl
questions.explain: The stakes attached to production — real customers, real data, real downtime cost — justify safeguards like required approvals that dev and staging don't need.
